title: The Multi-Agent Architecture That Actually Ships — Luke Alvoeiro, Factory
talk_summary: Factory's 'missions' system runs multi-day autonomous software projects using a three-role architecture (orchestrator/workers/validators) with a validation contract written before code, serial feature execution with read-only parallelism, and structured handoffs. The core insight is that validation must be adversarial and behavior-based, and that orchestration logic should live in prompts/skills rather than hard-coded state machines so it improves with each model release.

takeaways.what_they_do: During planning, before any code, the orchestrator writes a validation contract of hundreds of assertions defining correctness independently of implementation; each feature is assigned assertions it must satisfy and the sum of features must cover every assertion.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Tests written after implementation don't catch bugs. They confirm decisions.
takeaways.numbers: hundreds of assertions per complex project

takeaways.technique: Serial feature execution with read-only parallelism
takeaways.what_they_do: Only one worker or validator runs at a time per mission; parallelism is allowed only for read-only operations (codebase search, API research, parallel code-review agents within validation).

When a worker finishes, it fills a structured handoff: what was completed, what was left undone, commands run and their exit codes, issues discovered, and whether it followed orchestrator procedures. Milestone boundaries use these to scope corrective work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Not by hoping that agents remember what happened but by forcing them to write it down

takeaways.technique: Right model per role, cross-provider validation
takeaways.what_they_do: Planning uses slow careful reasoning models, implementation uses fast code-fluent models, validation uses precise instruction-followers; validation deliberately uses a different provider than implementation to avoid shared training-data bias.
takeaways.evidence_quote: validation might use a different model provider entirely to make sure that it's not biased by the same training data

takeaways.what_they_do: After each milestone, a separate validator spawns the running application and interacts with it via computer use — filling forms, clicking buttons, checking pages render — to verify end-to-end functional flows, in addition to lint/type/test/code-review scrutiny.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It spawns the application. It interacts with it through computer use ... ensures that functional flows work holistically.
takeaways.numbers: most wall-clock time is spent here, not generating tokens

takeaways.technique: Orchestration logic in prompts/skills, thin deterministic core
takeaways.what_they_do: Almost all orchestration logic (feature decomposition, failure handling, worker behavior) lives in ~700 lines of prompt/skill text defined per mission; deterministic code only does bookkeeping like running validation and blocking progress on unresolved handoff issues.
takeaways.evidence_quote: almost all of the orchestration logic is defined in prompts and skills ... instead of like a hard-coded state machine
takeaways.numbers: ~700 lines of text; four sentences can alter execution strategy dramatically
